output.initial_context:
RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

Ciarán Walsh is a self-contained, methodical man in his early forties who has lived alone for eight years in a small stone house on the edge of Galway. He works remotely for a Dublin software firm, spending his mornings at a laptop in his kitchen; colleagues know him only as an efficient voice who never turns on his camera. When a build fails, he says little but pushes a cleanly documented fix within the hour. He grew up in a farming family inland from Galway, where he learned early that dependency meant vulnerability. His quiet father repaired his own machinery and said little at the dinner table. At fifteen, when a summer storm collapsed a cattle shed, the family spent a week salvaging timber and re-setting the roof without asking neighbours for help. That week hardened something in him: he discovered he could fix almost anything by careful study, and he preferred to solve his own problems.

He values independence and self-reliance above all, and prefers to give help without being asked or acknowledged. He cannot stand to see a small failure go unrepaired. He has a sense of duty to his place. On weekends he sails his aging twenty-foot sloop alone, knowing every bolt, seam, and engine quirk. He never races and avoids marina social gatherings. He is polite to neighbours—a raised hand, a brief nod—but does not attend festivals, join committees, or stop for tea. Every Friday, without fail, he walks to the footbridge at the edge of the tidal marsh and replaces the broken step he noticed the week before, using a spare piece of treated oak and a handsaw. No one sees him, but the step is always solid. He gives without being asked, fixes what is broken without explanation. He wants to be left alone but also to matter; the footbridge step is his quiet compromise.

He is financially comfortable, with savings and a boat that needs new rigging but no intention to buy it. He has made peace with solitude, though he may linger when harbour lights come on or watch a child cross the bridge.

His only sibling is Aoife, eight years younger, living inland near Tuam. Their contact is a few short calls a year, mostly initiated by her. Two summers ago he helped her fit kitchen units and left before tea was poured, as she expected. She knows he prefers solitude and never pushes, but checks in when she is nearby. His established pattern with unexpected family calls is to let them ring and call back later the same evening. On the rare occasions he agrees to meet someone, he arrives early and keeps the conversation brief. He has declined casual neighbour invitations consistently, but has shown up for practical emergencies.

He is skilled at practical repairs—rewinding alternators, replacing shackles, patching hulls, fixing machinery—and proficient in software development with clean documentation. He is emotionally reserved, does not express feelings openly, and tends to give care through actions rather than words.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

On Saturday afternoon, Ciarán is in the shed re-winding an alternator when his phone buzzes. His younger sister, Aoife, who rarely calls, is on the line. She says she is driving back from a work trip and is passing through Galway, and is already at the petrol station near the footbridge. She has forty minutes before she needs to head inland to collect her kids from school. She asks if he can meet her there for a coffee. He can see the station roof from his garden. He is in the middle of a delicate solder job and has not showered since morning.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

He is kneeling on the shed floor, reheating a solder joint with steady, slightly tacky hands. He has not eaten since breakfast. His hair is flattened with sweat. The alternator is half-wound. He had planned to finish this winding, then walk to the footbridge to re-check the step he replaced last Friday.

The familiar ring of Aoife's number brings back the memory of her last call, which was to tell him about the children's school play. Looking toward the station roof, he remembers the Tuesday he saw her car parked there and assumed she was just filling up, only to learn later she had waited an hour hoping he would come out.
